title: Accessibility as a foundation for usable interaction
outcome: Check semantics, names, focus, contrast, motion, and zoom as part of the main flow.
useCase: Every reusable component and critical business flow.
benefits: Improves access and often clarifies interaction for everyone.
drawbacks: Custom widgets carry ongoing keyboard and semantics responsibilities.
version: Web UX · WCAG 2.2 · principles, not magic formulas
cue: Name it. Reach it. Operate it. Understand it.

trace.title: Semantic structure
trace.detail: Accessibility is not a final color check. A person must be able to perceive the state, operate controls, understand the result, and use compatible assistive technology. Native HTML gives many behaviors that a clickable div does not.

trace.title: Follow one item
trace.detail:
Complete the same task without a mouse. Can you reach every control, see focus, understand its name, operate it, and recover from failure? Then zoom the page and inspect reflow. Then test the key path with a screen reader.

Respect reduced-motion preferences for unnecessary animation. Avoid information conveyed only by color, hover, or movement.

trace.title: Try the failure
trace.detail: Adding role=button to a div without keyboard behavior creates a misleading contract. A focus trap that cannot be escaped is a defect. aria-hidden content can still contain focusable elements if implemented carelessly.

recallPrompt: Without notes: Check semantics, names, focus, contrast, motion, and zoom as part of the main flow. Explain one example and one failure.
